issues.issue: General Amendatory Endorsement No. 8 amends the Item 1 named insured to "Children's Health System, Inc." (singular), so the declarations and that endorsement identify the insured differently. The mismatch is minor but could matter to which corporate entity is the first named insured.

The declarations state an $18,000,000 each-occurrence limit but only a $9,000,000 aggregate, a facially incoherent pairing in which the aggregate is half the per-occurrence limit. A court would have to decide which figure governs a single large loss.

General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c122) states the policy limits are amended to $20,000,000 each occurrence and $20,000,000 aggregate, contradicting the $18,000,000/$9,000,000 shown here. Nothing reconciles the declarations figures with the endorsement figures.
"Short rate of earned premium" is used as a minimum-premium benchmark without any table or formula in the policy to compute it. The phrase's content must be supplied from outside the instrument.

The Contingent Excess Medical Malpractice endorsement (c111) makes contingent cover attach over underlying insurance "identified as being listed for contingency coverage purposes," but this Item 7 schedule identifies no policy in that way. The cross-reference has no referent in the schedule.

The grant turns entirely on "ultimate net loss," "retained limit" and "occurrence," each separately defined, so the reach of the indemnity is only as clear as those definitions. The phrase "to which this policy applies" adds a further undefined qualifier.

The grant covers "personal injury" broadly, while the Personal Injury Endorsement (c062) and the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089) strip out most hospital-related injury, leaving disagreement about what the insuring agreement actually delivers. A court would have to harmonise grant and endorsements.

The company "shall" defend suits not covered by underlying insurance but "may make such investigation negotiation and settlement ... as it deems expedient," mixing a mandatory duty with unfettered discretion. The boundary between the two is not drawn.

The Asbestos Exclusion (c088) expressly negates any duty to defend for asbestos suits, and the defence obligation here is conditioned on there being no underlying coverage, which the Schedule of Underlying Insurance (c007) supplies for most risks. Whether any defence duty survives is a question of fit.

The drop-down duty applies "only where this policy applies and is immediately in excess of underlying insurance listed on the declarations page without intervening insurance," a condition whose application depends on facts about other insurers' layers. "Exhausted by an occurrence" is also undefined as between payment and mere erosion.

Condition 13 (c059) says that if underlying insurance is not maintained the policy applies as if it had been, and Condition 5 (c045) requires the underlying limit actually to have been paid, which pull against this drop-down obligation. The three provisions must be reconciled to know when the company steps in.

"Any amount payable ... except settlement of claims or suits, is in addition to the ultimate net loss" is compressed to the point that the carve-out's reach is unclear. It is not obvious which supplementary payments fall inside the limit.

The definition of ultimate net loss (c024) already excludes loss and legal expenses, so the relationship between that exclusion and this "in addition to" sentence needs harmonising. A court could be asked whether expenses erode the limit.

The self-insured retention in Item 4 applies under the Retained Limit definition (c025) only when underlying insurance is inapplicable, yet this clause requires reimbursement of any ultimate net loss paid within the SIR without that qualification. When the SIR bites is left to be worked out between the two.

This paragraph III is superseded verbatim by the Aggregate Limits Endorsement (c091) and its Item 3 figure is then changed by General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c122), which refers to "the policy limits in Item 2." Which limit text and which figure controls is a question about the fit of these three provisions.

The aggregate applies only to loss "arising out of the products or completed operations hazards," so for a hospital risk it is unclear what, if anything, the declarations' aggregate figure limits. The proviso's scope against the general occurrence limit is genuinely contestable.

The Aggregate Limits Endorsement (c092) replaces this paragraph and extends the aggregate to "any professional liability hazard," a category absent here. The two texts of paragraph III state different aggregate triggers.

The Policy Territory Amended endorsements (c114 and c126) purport to amend "the Policy Territory provisions of the Hospital Professional Liability coverage part attached to the policy," but the only territory provision in this instrument is this worldwide clause and no such coverage part is attached. The amendment has no identifiable target.

The nuclear exclusion is a long enumerated list with its own internal definitions, and the workers' compensation limb reaches "disability benefits or similar law" — a catch-all whose reach beyond the named schemes is undefined. "Similar law" is the contestable term.

The named insured includes "any other organization coming under the named insured's control of which it assumes active management," and neither "control" nor "active management" is defined or measured. Whether an affiliate qualifies is precisely the kind of boundary question a court is asked to draw.

The Additional Named Insureds endorsement (c093) lists specific affiliates and says "no automatic coverage for entities newly acquired by any of them is extended hereby," which cuts against the automatic inclusion of controlled organisations in this definition. The two provisions treat affiliate coverage differently.

The text of the "insured" definition is so mangled that the classes of persons made insureds (executive officers, directors, stockholders, real-estate managers, automobile users) cannot be reliably read off the page. Who is an insured is the central question the words fail to answer.

The exclusion block runs several distinct exclusions together and its property-damage limb reaches property "in the care, custody or control of the insured to the extent the insured is under contract to provide insurance," a qualifier of uncertain scope. The sudden-and-accidental pollution proviso is likewise a contested term.

The Total Pollution Exclusion (c101) replaces the pollution limb of this block and the Care, Custody & Control Exclusion (c082) states a much broader property exclusion without the "under contract to provide insurance" qualifier. Which version governs must be worked out across the endorsements.

Sub-paragraph (5) makes an insured of "any other person or organization who is an insured under any policy of underlying insurance," an open-ended class defined by reference to documents not reproduced here. The reach of that class is contestable.

The Cross Suits Endorsement (c063) bars claims between Named Insureds, and this definition sweeps in a much wider group of "insureds" who are not Named Insureds, so which suits are barred depends on reconciling the two. The overlap is not addressed.

"Ultimate net loss" excludes all loss and legal expenses yet is defined as "the sum actually paid or payable in cash," leaving the treatment of amounts payable but unpaid open. Whether settlements without the company's written consent count is likewise unresolved on the face of it.

"Retained limit" is the greater of scheduled underlying limits plus "any other underlying insurance collectible by the insured" or the self-insured retention, and "collectible" is undefined (actual collection, or nominal availability). The amount the insured must absorb turns on that word.

Condition 5 (c045) makes liability attach only when "the amount of the underlying limit has been paid," while Condition 13 (c059) deems unmaintained underlying insurance to have been in force; the retained limit figure has to be squared with both. The three together do not state one rule for attachment.

"Personal injury" is defined to include "bodily injury, shock, mental anguish, sickness or disease" plus offence-type injuries, and there is no separate bodily-injury definition to mark the line. The composite definition invites argument about which limb a claim falls under.

The Personal Injury Endorsement (c062) deletes mental injury, mental anguish, shock, false arrest, libel and privacy from this definition, and the Exclusion of Discrimination (c086) deletes limb (5), so the definition as printed cannot be applied as written. What is left of "personal injury" is a live question.

"Occurrence" means an accident "including continuous or repeated exposure to conditions, which results, during the policy period," in injury "neither expected nor intended from the standpoint of the insured." Both the trigger timing and the expected-or-intended qualifier are classic points of genuine disagreement.

All exposure "to substantially the same general conditions existing at or emanating from one location or source" is deemed one occurrence, and "substantially the same general conditions" and "one ... source" have no measurable boundary. Number-of-occurrences is exactly what this phrase would be litigated over.

How this deeming rule interacts with the per-occurrence limit in c016/c091 and the aggregate in c017/c092 determines the total recoverable, and the provisions do not say which applies first. That interaction has to be resolved across clauses.

"Products hazard" is framed with "includes" rather than "means," so the enumerated conditions may not be exhaustive of the category. The switch between "personal injury" and "bodily injury" inside the same sentence adds to the uncertainty.

"Completed operations hazard" is also introduced by "includes," leaving open whether the listed conditions exhaust the term. Its practical content for a hospital insured is not apparent from the words.

The declarations state a premium of $29,890 while the Pay Plan Endorsement (c107) sets an instalment schedule and General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c122) contemplates an unstated "additional premium of $___." The premium "stated in the declarations" is therefore not the whole story.

Notice is due "whenever it appears that an occurrence is likely to involve indemnity under this policy" and must be given "as soon as practicable," both of which are open-textured triggers with no fixed period. Late-notice disputes turn precisely on those words.

The Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c079) provides that no failure of a pre-loss condition affects the company's obligation unless it increases the risk or contributes to the loss, which cuts against treating this notice duty as strictly enforced. The two must be read together to know the consequence of late notice.

The company may participate "when in the judgment of the company" an occurrence may involve damages in excess of a threshold, and the text of that threshold is illegible in the instrument. The condition cannot be applied as printed.

Liability does not attach "until the amount of the underlying limit has been paid by or on behalf of the insured," and whether a below-limits settlement or the insured's own funding satisfies that requirement is not addressed. Exhaustion language of this kind is regularly contested.

Condition 13 (c059) says that if underlying policies are not maintained the umbrella applies "in the same manner as it would have applied had such policies been maintained in force," which is difficult to square with a strict actual-payment attachment rule. The two conditions state different consequences for an unfilled underlying layer.

The insured must make claim "as soon as practicable" after paying loss or after liability is "finally determined," and neither phrase is given a period or a benchmark. The trigger for the claim clock is left open.

The clause is garbled to the point that the sequence of conditions for a third party to "recover under this policy" cannot be read off the page. What entitlement it confers is not ascertainable from the text.

The Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c072) deletes the "Action Against Company" condition "in its entirety" and replaces it with c072–c074, so whether this text survives at all is in question. Its continued operation depends on that endorsement.

The Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c072) deletes the "Action Against Company" condition in its entirety, and its replacement (c073) says "any person or organization ... shall be entitled to recover under this policy," which points the opposite way from this no-joinder bar. Whether the bar survives is a genuine question of fit.

The same bankruptcy sentence is repeated in the Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c074), so the policy contains duplicate provisions on the point. The duplication is harmless but leaves which text governs unstated.

The assignment condition is broken mid-sentence ("shall not bind ... unless canceled, shall cover the insured's legal ... unexpired portion of such period"), so the rule on assignment and on an insured's death cannot be extracted. As printed it states no operative rule.

The clause makes this policy excess over "any other valid and collectible insurance available to the insured, whether or not described in the Schedule of Underlying Insurance," then imposes a contribution formula for other excess indemnity policies. "Valid and collectible" and the parenthetical carve-out are the terms two insurers would read differently.

The Overlap Endorsement (c115) presupposes disputes between insurers over which policy applies and shifts the insured's expenses to this insurer, which sits awkwardly with this clause's blanket excess-and-contribution scheme. The two provisions allocate the consequences of overlapping cover differently.

The Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c075) adds that the company recovers "only after the insured has been fully compensated for damages," which qualifies this unconditional subrogation right. The two must be read together to know when subrogation attaches.

This apportionment reimburses the excess-paying interest first and only then the insured or underlying insurers, whereas the Wisconsin made-whole amendment (c075) entitles the company to recovery only after the insured is fully compensated. The order of payment stated in the two provisions conflicts.

This condition says notice to or knowledge of an agent works no waiver or change and that terms can be changed only by endorsement, while the Wisconsin Amendatory Endorsement (c076–c077) makes an agent's knowledge the company's knowledge and prevents a known breach from voiding the policy. The two state opposite rules about agent knowledge.

The Cancellation – Wisconsin endorsement (c066) restates cancellation by the named insured in different terms, so two cancellation-by-insured provisions sit in the same policy. Which controls is unstated.

This condition requires thirty days' written notice of company cancellation, while the Cancellation – Wisconsin endorsement (c067–c069) permits ten days and General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100) requires sixty days. Three different notice periods govern the same act.

The delivery-and-refund sentence is broken into fragments ("shall be sufficient ... any refund due the named insured") and neither the proof-of-mailing rule nor the refund calculation can be read from it. As printed it states no ascertainable rule about premium refund.

The insured warrants that underlying policies or "renewals or replacements thereof not more restricted" will be maintained, and "not more restricted" has no benchmark for comparison. Whether a replacement policy breaches the warranty turns on that phrase.

The deeming rule here (the umbrella applies as if underlying insurance had been maintained) cannot easily be squared with Condition 5 (c045), which withholds attachment until the underlying limit is actually paid. The consequence of a gap in the underlying layer is stated twice, differently.

"Except insofar as coverage is available to the insured in the underlying insurance listed" is a following-form qualifier whose reach depends on what "available" means once the underlying limits are exhausted or the underlying insurer denies. "Liability assumed ... under any contract or agreement" is itself a contested phrase.

The endorsement preserves cover "insofar as coverage is afforded under the underlying insurance or self insured retention listed in Item 7 of the Declarations," but Item 7 is the schedule of underlying insurance and the self-insured retention appears in Item 4. The mis-cited item makes the carve-back's operation uncertain.

This endorsement removes mental injury, mental anguish, shock, false arrest, malicious prosecution, libel and privacy invasion from "personal injury," which the policy's own definition (c026) expressly includes. The definition and the endorsement point in opposite directions.

The exclusion bars claims "initiated, alleged or caused to be brought about by a Named Insured ... against any other Named Insured," and "caused to be brought about" has no clear boundary. Whether a claim assigned or encouraged by one insured is caught is left open.

The policy creates several tiers of insured — Named Insureds (c093), additional insureds (c096) and persons who are insureds only under underlying policies (c023) — and this endorsement speaks only of "Named Insured," so its reach across those tiers is unresolved. The definitional structure and the exclusion do not line up.

This proviso operates only "if this policy applies to professional liability," yet the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089) excludes professional health care services altogether subject to its own exception (c090). Whether the condition is ever satisfied cannot be answered from this clause alone.

Condition 12 (c055) also provides for cancellation by the named insured in different words, leaving two overlapping provisions on the same subject. Which text governs surrender versus mailed notice is unstated.

The ten-day notice permitted here conflicts with the thirty days in Condition 12 (c056) and the sixty days promised by General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100). The policy states three different periods for company cancellation.

General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100) promises sixty days' written notice "in the event of cancellation or non-renewal" without excepting non-payment, which contradicts the ten-day period allowed here. The two notice rules cannot both apply to a premium default.

Cancellation is permitted for "substantial change in the risk assumed" and "substantial breaches of contractual duties, conditions or warranties," neither of which is given any measure of substantiality. The grounds are stated at a level of generality that would have to be construed.

The ten-day period stated here conflicts with the sixty-day notice guaranteed by General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c100) and with the thirty days in Condition 12 (c056). The three provisions give different answers for the same mid-term cancellation.

This paragraph addresses policies "written without a fixed expiration date or for a policy term longer than one year," but the declarations (c004) fix a one-year term, so it has no application to this policy. The mismatch is apparent but consequence-free.

The insured is given "a right to renewal of this policy on the terms then being applied by the Company to similar risks," and neither "similar risks" nor the terms so applied are ascertainable from the instrument. The content of the renewal right is left open.

This makes "full compliance by the insured with all the terms of this policy" a condition precedent to suit, while the Declarations paragraph of the same endorsement (c079) says no failure of a pre-loss condition affects the company's obligation unless it increases the risk or contributes to the loss. The two paragraphs of one endorsement state opposite consequences for breach.

"Any person or organization or the legal representative thereof shall be entitled to recover under this policy" is unqualified and appears to give strangers to the contract a direct right of recovery. The absence of any limiting words is the defect.

This entitlement sits against the no-joinder sentence (c048), which bars any person from joining the company in an action, and against the full-compliance condition precedent (c072) in the same endorsement. Whether third parties may sue directly cannot be answered without reconciling all three.

The made-whole rule contradicts the apportionment order in Condition 10 (c053), which reimburses the excess-paying interest first and the insured only out of any remaining balance. The two cannot both control the distribution of a recovery.

Imputing an agent's knowledge to the company is the opposite of Condition 11 (c054), which provides that notice to or knowledge of any agent works no waiver or change. The two provisions state incompatible rules.

The provision repeats the preceding agent-knowledge sentence before adding the non-avoidance rule, so the same words appear twice within one clause. The duplication obscures which sentence carries the operative rule.

The rule that a breach known to the agent "shall not void the policy or defeat a recovery" cannot be squared with the condition-precedent requirement of full compliance in c072. One forgives known breaches, the other bars suit for any breach.

This provision forgives failures of pre-loss conditions unless they increase the risk or contribute to the loss, directly cutting across the "full compliance ... condition precedent" requirement in c072 and the notice condition in c041. The policy states two inconsistent consequences for breach of condition.

The exclusion reaches acts or omissions "of any insured subject of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act ... with respect to their duties under pension or Employee benefit plans," and the mangled "insured subject of" leaves the class of excluded actors unclear. Whether it is fiduciary status or plan-related duty that triggers the exclusion is not stated cleanly.

Limb (b) excludes damage to "property used by any Insured hereunder" without any qualification, an extraordinarily broad category next to the narrower owned/occupied and care-custody-control limbs. The general limb's reach against the specific ones is genuinely contestable.

The base policy exclusion (c022) limits the care, custody or control exclusion to property "to the extent the insured is under contract to provide insurance," a qualifier this endorsement drops. The two versions of the property exclusion differ in scope.

The endorsement says "directors and officers are excluded from this contract for liability arising out of wrongful acts," which reads as excluding persons rather than a class of loss. Whether it removes D&Os as insureds or only removes a category of liability is left ambiguous.

The exception in c085 preserves liability for personal injury, bodily injury, property damage, hospital professional liability and advertisers' liability — essentially everything the policy insures — so the exclusion may have nothing left to operate on. The exclusion and its exception have to be reconciled.

"Wrongful Acts" ends with "or any other matter claimed against them solely by reason of their being directors or officers," a catch-all appended to a list of specific errors and breaches of duty. How far that residual clause reaches beyond the enumerated conduct is the classic ejusdem generis question.

The carve-out restores cover for personal injury, bodily injury, property damage and hospital professional liability, which are the only categories of liability the insuring agreement (c009) covers, so read literally it nullifies the D&O exclusion in c083. The exclusion and exception cannot both be given full effect.

The policy's definition of personal injury (c026(5)) expressly includes "racial or religious discrimination not committed by or on behalf of the insured," which this endorsement wholly removes. The definition and the endorsement point in opposite directions on discrimination claims.

The exclusion's opening words are cut off and the sentence reaches injury "at any time of the manufacture of, or mining of, or use of, or exposure to Asbestos products," leaving the excluded conduct only partially legible. What the exclusion applies to cannot be stated confidently from the text.

The insuring agreement (c010) obliges the company to defend suits not covered by underlying insurance "even if such suit is groundless, false or fraudulent," while this endorsement negates any defence duty for asbestos allegations. The two set different rules for a suit alleging asbestos injury.

The exclusion turns on injury "arising out of the rendering of or failure to render" professional health care services, and the line between professional services and administrative or corporate negligence by a hospital is a standing point of dispute. Limb (b)'s "similar professional board or committee" is a further catch-all of uncertain reach.

Other provisions assume this policy does cover professional liability — the Cross Suits professional-liability proviso (c064), the Aggregate Limits Endorsement's "any professional liability hazard" (c092), the D&O exception's "hospital professional liability" (c085) and the professional liability limits endorsement (c134). A blanket professional services exclusion cannot easily be reconciled with them.

The exception is framed as a double negative — the exclusion "does not apply to those entities or individuals that are not subject to the Wisconsin Patients Compensation Fund" — and "subject to" could mean statutorily required to participate, actually enrolled, or in fact covered for the claim. The class of insureds who keep professional cover turns entirely on that phrase.

The Contingent Excess Medical Malpractice endorsement (c109–c111) draws the same line by reference to Wis. Stat. § 655.001 and its own contingency conditions, and c113 disapplies a differently dated version of this form. Which instrument governs Fund-related entities is not resolved.

This endorsement amends paragraph III to a figure "stated in Item 3 of the declarations," while General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c122) purports to amend "the policy limits in Item 2" to $20,000,000. The two amendments to the limit provision do not reference the same declarations item or the same figure.

The aggregate is extended to loss arising out of "any professional liability hazard," a term that — unlike "products hazard" and "completed operations hazard" — is nowhere defined in the policy. Its reach against those two defined companions is exactly the general-versus-specific problem.

Applying an aggregate to professional liability presupposes that professional liability is covered, which the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089) denies except for entities outside the Wisconsin Fund. The two endorsements cannot both be given their natural reading.

The definition of named insured (c020) automatically includes any subsidiary and any organisation under the named insured's control, whereas this endorsement lists entities individually and denies automatic coverage for newly acquired entities. The two provisions state different rules for affiliate coverage.

Cover for the listed additional insureds runs "only with respect to their interest in the operations of the Named Insured," and several entries describe the insurable interest merely as "As their interest may appear." The extent of each entity's cover is left to be inferred rather than stated.

Seeger Health Resources, Inc. appears both as a Named Insured under c093 and as a mere additional insured here with cover limited to its interest as lessor, so its status under the policy is stated twice and differently. Which characterisation governs is unresolved.

This endorsement restricts the Collection Agency Errors and Omissions Exclusion to Med-Health Financial Services, whereas the form itself (c108) excludes such acts "by or on behalf of the Insured" generally. The scope of that exclusion is stated inconsistently by the two documents.

The sixty-day notice promised here conflicts with the thirty days in Condition 12 (c056) and with the ten-day periods in the Cancellation – Wisconsin endorsement (c067, c068, c069). The policy gives three inconsistent cancellation notice periods.

The exclusion turns on "pollutants" discharged at or from premises owned, occupied, rented or loaned to any insured, a formulation whose application to ordinary indoor substances in a hospital is a standing point of argument. "Actual, alleged or threatened ... seepage, migration" further widens an already open trigger.

The endorsement replaces the base pollution exclusion in c022, which excluded only discharges that were not "sudden and accidental"; the replacement drops that qualifier entirely. Which formulation applies to a given claim depends on reading the two together.

A hostile fire is defined as one "which becomes uncontrollable or breaks out from where it was intended to be," leaving the friendly/hostile line to be drawn case by case. The definition restates the ambiguity rather than resolving it.

The clause excludes loss, cost or expense arising out of any "request, demand or order" to respond to pollutants, and whether an informal agency letter is a "request" of that kind is not settled by the words. The catch-all "in any way respond to" compounds it.

"Pollutants" is defined as "any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant or contaminant, including smoke, vapor, soot, fumes, acids, alkalis, chemicals and waste," a general definition trailing a list of industrial specifics. Whether the general words reach substances unlike the listed ones is precisely the general-versus-specific dispute.

The schedule totals the $29,890 premium shown in Item 5, but General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c122) raises the limits "in consideration of the additional premium of $___" with the figure left blank, so the pay plan no longer matches the consideration. The instalment schedule and the endorsement premium cannot both be complete.

General Amendatory Endorsement No. 2 (c098) attaches this form "only as respects Med-Health Financial Services," while the form itself excludes collection-agency errors of "the Insured" without limitation. The two texts state different scopes for the same exclusion.

Coverage is withheld for "any entity which is defined by Wisconsin Statute, Section 655.001 as a health care provider," which imports a statutory classification whose application to particular corporate insureds is contestable. Whether an entity falls within the statutory definition is the operative question.

The Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089–c090) draws the professional-liability line by a different test — whether the entity is "subject to the Wisconsin Patients Compensation Fund" — so two endorsements exclude overlapping but differently defined groups. Which test governs a given insured is unresolved.

The statutory definition is "interpreted to include subsidiaries of holding companies of the named insured," a phrase that reverses the ordinary corporate relationship and does not identify whose holding companies are meant. The class of entities swept in cannot be identified with confidence.

Contingent cover depends on an entity that "adheres to the definition of health care provider" being "nevertheless disallowed coverage" by the Fund, and neither "adheres to" nor "disallowed coverage" has a settled meaning. The trigger for the whole contingency turns on those words.

The clause applies the cover over underlying insurance "identified as being listed for contingency coverage purposes," but Item 7 of the declarations (c007) contains no such identification. The condition points to a designation that does not exist in the instrument.

The clause disapplies "Form No. 035(12/87) Professional Services Excluded," but the professional services exclusion actually attached to this policy is Form 035 WI (1/94). The mis-cited form number leaves it uncertain whether the disapplication reaches the form in force.

If the reference is read as ineffective, the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089) would continue to bar the very cover the contingent-excess endorsement (c111) purports to grant. The two provisions would then cancel each other out.

General Amendatory Endorsement No. 5 (c124) deletes Form 009-118 (10/92) as "null and void" and substitutes the 2/96 version (c126), yet this endorsement remains in the policy and on the endorsement schedule. It also amends a "Hospital Professional Liability coverage part" that is not attached to this umbrella policy.

The insurer indemnifies "any legal or other expenses necessarily incurred" by the insured in determining which insurer bears the loss, and "necessarily incurred" and "other expenses" are left without any measure. The scope of the reimbursable expense is open.

The definition of ultimate net loss (c024) expressly excludes all loss and legal expenses, and Condition 9 (c051) makes this policy excess over other collectible insurance; this endorsement promises the insured legal expenses of insurer disputes. The provisions treat coverage-dispute costs inconsistently.

Indemnity is payable "only if it is determined that payment of said loss shall be rendered under this policy," which conditions reimbursement of the very expenses of determining coverage on the outcome of that determination. The circularity leaves the promise's practical content unclear.

General Amendatory Endorsement No. 5 (c124) states that Form 009-133 is "deleted from the policy and considered null and void," yet this Trebled Damages Exclusion remains attached and on the endorsement schedule. Whether it forms part of the contract is a question about the fit of the two documents.

The clause first excludes trebled damages and then promises payment of "one-third of the total sum which the insured is obligated to pay," a formula that assumes an exact trebling and does not address mixed awards. The interaction of the exclusion and the one-third payment is not spelled out.
This paragraph is part of Form 009-133, which General Amendatory Endorsement No. 5 (c124) declares deleted and null and void. Its operative force depends entirely on that deletion.

This definition belongs to Form 009-133, which General Amendatory Endorsement No. 5 (c124) deletes from the policy as null and void, while the form remains physically attached. Whether the narrowed meaning of "damages" operates at all turns on that conflict.

The endorsement amends "the policy limits in Item 2," but Item 2 of the declarations is the policy period and the limits appear in Item 3; the consideration is also left blank as "the additional premium of $___." Both defects go to whether and on what terms the limits were changed.

The $20,000,000/$20,000,000 limits stated here contradict the $18,000,000 each occurrence and $9,000,000 aggregate shown in Items 3–5 of the declarations (c005), which are unaltered elsewhere. Which set of limits governs is a direct conflict between the two documents.

The forms said to be "deleted from the policy and considered null and void" — 009-133 (c118–c120) and 009-118 (10/92) (c114) — remain physically attached to the policy and listed on the Schedule of Endorsements. The deletion and the assembled instrument contradict each other.

This replacement endorsement amends "the Policy Territory provisions of the Hospital Professional Liability coverage part attached to the policy," but no such coverage part is attached to this umbrella policy, whose territory clause (c018) applies worldwide. The amendment has no target within the instrument.

The endorsement states an Effective Date of Endorsement of 07/08/1996 but its text says it is "effective on the inception date of the policy unless otherwise stated herein." The two dates in the same document point different ways for the added insured's cover.

Adding Children's Specialty Group, Inc. to Form 009-052 gives it named insured status, which interacts with the Cross Suits Endorsement (c063) and the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c090) in ways this endorsement does not address. The effective date of that status is also left to c127.

The endorsement's stated Effective Date is 01/01/1997 while its own text makes it "effective on the inception date of the policy unless otherwise stated herein." The internal date conflict matters to when CMG – Brown Deer Campus became insured.

This endorsement adds CMG – Brown Deer Campus "as a Named Insured" in the policy generally, whereas the parallel endorsements (c128, c133) add campuses to Form 009-052; the routes to named insured status are stated inconsistently. Which mechanism governs, and with it the effect of c093's no-automatic-coverage sentence, is unaddressed.

The named insured is amended to "Children's Health System, Inc." whereas the declarations (c001) and every endorsement heading say "Children's Health Systems, Inc." The identity of the first named insured is stated two ways in the same instrument.

Limits are increased for "those individuals and/or entities to whom this coverage applies and that are not subject to the Wisconsin Patients Compensation Fund," repeating the undefined "subject to the Fund" test and adding an unexplained "to whom this coverage applies." The class of beneficiaries cannot be fixed from the words.

The endorsement is headed to policy HPP-1996-4104-00, the underlying comprehensive general liability policy in Item 7, yet it appears in this umbrella file and speaks of professional liability limits that the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c089) excludes here. Whether it operates on this policy at all is a genuine question.
